title: Command Line: Your Powerful Toolbox
description: Learn to direct your computer, move around your project, and run Python from the terminal.

lessons.title: Meet the terminal
lessons.content:
The terminal is a text-based way to give instructions to your computer. In VS Code, open it with Terminal > New Terminal.

A terminal runs a shell (such as Bash, zsh, or PowerShell). Python is a programming language that you can run from the shell. They are related tools, but they are not the same thing.

Try these safe commands in your own terminal:

pwd       Show the current folder (PowerShell also supports this)
ls        List files (PowerShell: dir)
python --version   Show the installed Python version (Windows may use py --version)

A command is made of a program and, sometimes, extra information called arguments. Press Enter to run it. Use the up-arrow key to revisit a previous command.
exercises: Write Python code that prints a friendly message. Download it as hello.py, then run it in your terminal with python hello.py (Windows: py hello.py).

lessons.title: Move around your project
lessons.content:
Commands work in a current folder. Knowing where you are and how to move between folders helps you run the right files.

pwd       Show the current folder
ls        List files in this folder (PowerShell: dir)
cd folder-name   Move into a folder
cd ..     Move up one folder
mkdir practice   Create a folder named practice

Use ls (or dir) after moving to check where you are. These navigation commands are safe ways to explore. Be careful with commands you do not recognize, especially commands that delete or overwrite files.
exercises: Write a Python script that prints a three-step checklist for opening a project folder in the terminal.

lessons.title: Run Python from the terminal
lessons.content:
Save a Python program in a file ending in .py. In the terminal, move to the folder containing the file, then run it:

python hello.py

On many Windows installations, use py hello.py instead. Python can also run useful standard-library tools with the -m option, for example:

python -m unittest

If a command is unfamiliar, python --help shows Python's command options. This learning page runs your code inside your browser; use Download .py to save your solution before trying it in your own terminal.
exercises: Write a Python script that prints the command you would use to run a file named practice.py.

title: Python fundamentals
description: Start with values, variables, strings, numbers, input, and output.

lessons.title: First steps
lessons.content:
A variable gives a value a name. Python can store text, whole numbers, and decimal numbers.

Example:
name = "Ada"
age = 12
print(f"Hello, {name}! Next year you will be {age + 1}.")

The f before a string lets you put expressions inside braces.
exercises: Store your name and favorite hobby in variables and print a sentence.

lessons.title: Numbers and math
lessons.content:
Python handles whole numbers (int) and decimals (float). You can add, subtract, multiply, and divide using +, -, *, and /. Use // for whole-number division and % for the remainder.

Example:
apples = 7
people = 2
print(apples // people)  # 3
print(apples % people)   # 1
exercises: Convert a distance from kilometers to miles (multiply by 0.621371).

lessons.title: Working with strings
lessons.content:
Strings are text inside quotes. You can join them with +, repeat them with *, and measure their length with len().

Example:
first = "Python"
last = "Rocks"
print(first + " " + last)
print(len(first))
exercises: Ask for a temperature in Celsius and print its Fahrenheit conversion.

title: Decisions and loops
description: Make choices with conditions and repeat work with loops.

lessons.title: Choose and repeat
exercises: Ask for an age and label the person as a child, teen, or adult.

lessons.title: While loops
lessons.content:
A while loop repeats as long as a condition is true. Be careful: if the condition never becomes false, the loop runs forever.

Example:
count = 3
while count > 0:
    print(count)
    count = count - 1
print("Blast off!")
exercises: Make a number guessing game with a fixed secret number.

lessons.title: Breaking and continuing
exercises: Print numbers from 1 to 20 and label each even or odd.

title: Collections
description: Group related data with lists, dictionaries, sets, and tuples.

lessons.title: Grouping data
lessons.content:
Lists keep an ordered collection. Dictionaries associate keys with values. Sets keep unique values.

Example:
shopping = ["apples", "bread"]
shopping.append("tea")
scores = {"Ari": 8, "Bo": 10}
print(shopping)
print(scores["Ari"])
exercises: Make a shopping list, add and remove an item, then print each item.

lessons.title: Dictionaries
lessons.content:
A dictionary stores pairs of keys and values. Access a value by its key. Use .get() to avoid errors when a key might be missing.

Example:
person = {"name": "Ada", "age": 36}
print(person["name"])
print(person.get("city", "Unknown"))
exercises: Make a dictionary of names and phone numbers.

lessons.title: Tuples and sets
lessons.content:
A tuple is like a list you cannot change (immutable). A set stores unique values and has no order.

Example:
coordinates = (10, 20)
unique_tags = {"python", "code", "python"}
print(coordinates)
print(unique_tags)  # set removes the duplicate
exercises: Count how often each word appears in a sentence.

title: Functions
description: Give reusable behavior a name and split problems into smaller steps.

lessons.title: Reusable behavior
lessons.content:
Functions accept inputs through parameters and can send a result back with return.

Example:
def rectangle_area(width, height):
    return width * height

area = rectangle_area(4, 3)
print(area)
exercises: Write a function that converts Celsius to Fahrenheit.

lessons.title: Default arguments
lessons.content:
You can give parameters default values. If the caller does not provide that argument, the default is used.

Example:
def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    return f"{greeting}, {name}!"

print(greet("Ada"))
print(greet("Ada", "Hi"))
exercises: Write a function that takes a name and a greeting, with a default greeting.

lessons.title: Scope
lessons.content:
Variables created inside a function are local to that function. Variables created outside functions are global. It is best to pass data in as parameters and return results, rather than relying on globals.

Example:
def double(number):
    result = number * 2
    return result

print(double(5))
exercises: Write a function that returns a value, then call it and print the result.

title: Modules and errors
description: Organize code and handle what goes wrong.

lessons.title: Importing
lessons.content:
A module is a file containing Python code. Use import to bring it into your program. Python has a large standard library.

Example:
import math
print(math.sqrt(16))

You can also import specific functions:
from random import randint
print(randint(1, 10))
exercises: Import the math module and print the square root of 144.

lessons.title: Common errors
lessons.content:
Errors tell you what went wrong. TypeError means the wrong type of data. NameError means a variable is missing. IndexError means a list position is out of range.

Example:
# numbers = [1, 2]
# print(numbers[5])  <-- IndexError

Read the error message carefully; it usually tells you exactly what to fix.
exercises: Write code that triggers a TypeError, then fix it.

lessons.title: try / except
exercises: Ask for a number and handle the error if the user types text.

title: Files and data
description: Read from and write to files on your computer.

lessons.title: Reading files
lessons.content:
Use open() to read a file. Always close the file, or use with to close it automatically.

Example:
with open("notes.txt", "r") as file:
    content = file.read()
    print(content)
exercises: Create a file named hello.txt, write text to it, then read it back.

lessons.title: Writing files
lessons.content:
Open a file with "w" to write (this overwrites the file). Open with "a" to append.

Example:
with open("notes.txt", "w") as file:
    file.write("Hello\n")
exercises: Append your name to a file, then read the file to prove it worked.

lessons.title: JSON data
lessons.content:
JSON is a text format for structured data. Python can read and write JSON with the json module.

Example:
import json
data = {"name": "Ada", "age": 36}
text = json.dumps(data)
print(text)

parsed = json.loads(text)
print(parsed["name"])
exercises: Create a dictionary, convert it to JSON, then convert it back to a dictionary.

title: Object-oriented Python
description: Model things with classes and objects.

lessons.title: Classes and objects
exercises: Write a class called Book with a title and author, then create an instance.

lessons.title: Methods
exercises: Add a method to your Book class that prints a summary.

lessons.title: Inheritance
exercises: Create an Animal class, then a Dog class that inherits from it.

title: Testing
description: Learn to check your code with assertions and unit tests.

lessons.title: Why testing
lessons.content:
Tests prove your code works. Instead of clicking around manually, you write small programs that check if your functions return the right answers. This lets you change code without fear.

Example:
assert 2 + 2 == 4
print("Math works!")
exercises: Write three assert statements that verify basic math operations.

lessons.title: The unittest module
exercises: Write a unittest class that tests a multiply function.

lessons.title: Test-driven development
lessons.content:
TDD means writing the test first, watching it fail, then writing code to make it pass. This forces you to think about the interface before the implementation.

1. Write a failing test.
2. Write the simplest code to pass it.
3. Refactor safely.
exercises: Write a test for a function, see it fail, then write the function.
